questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation 

$$
{y}^{′}+5y=3{e}^{-5x},
$$

has the complementary solution ${y}_{c}(x)=A{e}^{-5x}$, find the particular solution to the equation.

${y}_{p}(x)=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
To find the general solution of an inhomogeneous first-order linear equation with constant coefficients on the left-hand side, we must find the sum of the complementary and particular solutions.

We see that the right-hand side is $3{e}^{-5x},$ and ${e}^{-5x}$ is a term in the complementary solution, so we assume that a particular solution takes the form 

$$
{y}_{p}=\alpha x{e}^{-5x},
$$

where $\alpha $ is a constant that is to be determined.

We calculate the first derivative of ${y}_{p}$ using the product rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{p}^{′} & =(\alpha x{e}^{-5x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha (x{e}^{-5x})^{′} \\  & =\alpha ({e}^{-5x}-5x{e}^{-5x}) \\  & =\alpha (1-5x){e}^{-5x}\end{aligned}
$$

To find the value of $\alpha ,$ we substitute ${y}_{p}$ and ${y}_{p}^{′}$ into the differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}(\alpha (1-5x){e}^{-5x})+5\alpha x{e}^{-5x} & =3{e}^{-5x} \\ (1-5x+5x)\alpha {e}^{-5x} & =3{e}^{-5x} \\ \alpha {e}^{-5x} & =3{e}^{-5x} \\ \alpha  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the particular solution ${y}_{p}(x)$ is

$$
{y}_{p}(x)=3x{e}^{-5x}.
$$

questions.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(3{e}^{x}+1)\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Which differential equation describes this motion?
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14157883/assets/785776cee4f82c5bfa5e86b5b1cb746b7c80f2d702fb52f67055a60bdff249ae.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(3{e}^{x}+1)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=3{e}^{x}+1.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=3{e}^{x}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we have

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=3{e}^{x}+1.\,\,(∗)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({v}^{2})=2v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(∗)$ as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=3{e}^{x}+1.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the matrices given below. Given that $A$ and $B$ are row equivalent matrices and $det(A)=6$, find $det(B).$

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -1 \\ -2 & 2 & -2 \\ -5 & 6 & 3\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 & -1 \\ -5 & 6 & 3 \\ -2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]?
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that $B$ can be obtained from $A$ by swapping the $2$nd and the $3$rd rows. 

This changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.
Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(B) & =-det(A) \\  & =-(6) \\  & =-6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: For the function $f(x,y,z)=z-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3,$ find the equation of the level surface $f(x,y,z)=3.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the level surfaces for the function $f(x,y,z)$ are given by the equation

$$
f(x,y,z)=c.
$$

In our case, we're interested in $c=3.$ So, we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =c \\ z-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3 & =3 \\ z & ={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the level surface for $c=3$ is the paraboloid $z={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$

questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F=(x+y)^{2}\,i+(y+z)^{2}\,j+(x+z)^{2}\,k.$ Evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(-2,1,-1).$
questions.worked_solution:
If $F=P\,i+Q\,j+R\,k$ is a vector field on ${R}^{3}$ and the partial derivatives of the components of $F$ all exist, then the divergence of $F$ is the scalar field given by

$$
\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F=\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z}.
$$

  

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}∇\cdot F & =\frac{∂P}{∂x}+\frac{∂Q}{∂y}+\frac{∂R}{∂z} \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((x+y)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂y}((y+z)^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂z}((x+z)^{2}) \\  & =2(x+y)+2(y+z)+2(x+z) \\  & =4(x+y+z).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate $\text{div}\,F$ at the point $(-2,1,-1),$ and obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{div}\,F(-2,1,-1) & =4((-2)+(1)+(-1)) \\  & =4\cdot (-2) \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Using the values in the table, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P((X,Y)\in \{(2,3),(2,6)\}) & =P((X,Y)=(2,3))+P((X,Y)=(2,6)) \\  & =f(2,3)+f(2,6) \\  & =0.25+0.5 \\  & =0.75.\end{aligned}
$$
